strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing real pain points in 3D content creation where UV mapping is time-consuming and requires both technical precision and artistic judgment
Sound technical approach combining semantic awareness via Shape Diameter Function partitioning with visibility awareness via ambient occlusion in a principled differentiable framework
Comprehensive evaluation including comparisons against multiple strong baselines (FlexPara, Autodesk Maya, Blender SmartUV, xatlas) with both qualitative and quantitative metrics
Strong qualitative results clearly demonstrating improvements in seam placement in occluded regions and semantic alignment with 3D part structure across diverse mesh types
Thorough documentation and reproducibility: public code availability, detailed algorithm descriptions, extensive appendices, and clear mathematical formulations (Eqs. 1-8)

Thoughtful two-stage pipeline design that separates geometry-preserving learning from task-specific objectives, with clear loss function design including wrapping, cycle-consistency, anti-overlap, and distortion penalties
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (SDF partitioning from Shapira et al. 2008, ambient occlusion from Zhukov et al. 1998, bi-directional cycle mapping from recent work) rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas

Quantitative improvements are often modest, particularly for geometry preservation metrics (conformality, equareality in Table 1) and semantic alignment metrics show only incremental gains over baselines

Absent user studies for validating perceptual quality claims—the core motivation about visibility is inherently perceptual, yet results are primarily visual inspection without psychophysical evaluation

Methodological concerns: soft seam membership scoring (Eq. 6) appears heuristic without sensitivity analysis; simple grid-based aggregation strategy lacks justification; SDF partitioning may fail on thin structures or complex topologies

Incomplete ablation studies—Table 5 ablates high-level objectives but lacks ablations on architectural choices, loss term weights, hyperparameter sensitivity, or comparison of alternative visibility proxies

Evaluation scope limitations: no dataset size/diversity reporting, missing computational cost analysis and runtime comparisons, no failure case analysis, no broader evaluation beyond external UV parameterization
Narrow scope focused specifically on UV mapping for mesh texturing with unclear applicability to other surface parameterization problems or broader geometry understanding tasks

Baseline concerns: FlexPara (2025) is very recent and not well-established; includes heuristic tools (Blender SmartUV) rather than purely learning-based comparisons; missing comparisons with other recent neural approaches

strengths: Well-motivated semantic-aware and visibility-aware objectives that address genuine shortcomings in existing mesh parameterization methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including user study with 115 participants, comparisons against commercial tools and recent baselines, quantitative metrics, and thorough ablations
Fully unsupervised and end-to-end differentiable framework requiring no labeled training data
Strong empirical results with visibly better parameterizations and seams placed in less-noticeable regions compared to baselines
Practical significance for 3D content creation, addressing a real industry bottleneck confirmed by surveys
Code will be made publicly available, enhancing reproducibility
Clear presentation with informative figures and logical paper structure
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - individual components (bi-directional cycle mapping, Shape Diameter Function, ambient occlusion) are from existing work; novelty is primarily in combining them with two new loss terms, which feels incremental

Significant computational overhead: semantic-aware pipeline is much slower than FlexPara; visibility-aware pipeline incurs ~90% additional overhead due to AO computation and seam extraction, with insufficient cost-benefit analysis
Heavy dependence on initial mesh segmentation quality with limited discussion of failure modes, robustness to different shape types, or behavior when segmentation is poor
Visibility objective uses ambient occlusion as indirect proxy for perceptuality; doesn't account for varying lighting conditions or viewpoints; AO computation itself is expensive

Insufficient exploration of trade-offs between multiple objectives (Eq. 8); relative loss weights not thoroughly ablated; potential conflicts between distortion minimization and semantic/visibility objectives not deeply analyzed
Limited comparison with recent learning-based methods - only one recent neural baseline (FlexPara 2025); most comparisons are against traditional or commercial methods
User study limitations: 11 comparisons per participant, limited shape diversity, no evaluation under different lighting/rendering conditions
Missing ablations on loss hyperparameters, insufficient sensitivity analysis, and limited discussion of failure cases and when method underperforms
Scalability questions: most results on simple-to-moderate shapes; unclear performance on millions-of-triangle meshes; no explicit complexity scaling analysis
Seam visibility metric (mean AO of seam vertices) is indirect and indirect; lacks direct perceptual validation or strong correlation analysis with actual seam perceptibility
Dense presentation with critical implementation details in lengthy appendix (14+ pages); some design choices (soft seam membership, loss weights) not sufficiently justified
Concurrent nature of FlexPara comparison raises questions about fair evaluation and development timeline
